sources.title: Multiomics analysis reveals the presence of a microbiome in the gut of fetal lambs.
sources.text:
Multiomics analysis reveals the presence of a microbiome in the gut of fetal lambs.
Microbial exposure is critical to neonatal and infant development, growth and immunity. However, whether a microbiome is present in the fetal gut prior to birth remains debated. In this study, lambs delivered by aseptic hysterectomy at full term were used as an animal model to investigate the presence of a microbiome in the prenatal gut using a multiomics approach.
Lambs were euthanised immediately after aseptic caesarean section and their cecal content and umbilical cord blood samples were aseptically acquired. Cecal content samples were assessed using metagenomic and metatranscriptomic sequencing to characterise any existing microbiome. Both sample types were analysed using metabolomics in order to detect microbial metabolites.

sources.text:
Molecular characterization of a bacteriophage (Chp2) from Chlamydia psittaci.
Comparisons of the proteome of abortifacient Chlamydia psittaci isolates from sheep by two-dimensional gel electrophoresis identified a novel abundant protein with a molecular mass of 61.4 kDa and an isoelectric point of 6.41. C-terminal sequence analysis of this protein yielded a short peptide sequence that had an identical match to the viral coat protein (VP1) of the avian chlamydiaphage Chp1. Electron microscope studies revealed the presence of a 25-nm-diameter bacteriophage (Chp2) with no apparent spike structures. Thin sections of chlamydia-infected cells showed that Chp2 particles were located to membranous structures surrounding reticulate bodies (RBs), suggesting that Chp2 is cytopathic for ovine C. psittaci RBs. {"markdown":"# PhiX174 genome organization

## Reference and architecture

The current RefSeq, **NC_001422.1**, is a **5,386-nt circular ssDNA** genome annotated with 11 genes. This supersedes the historical description of approximately **5,375 nt** and

the older GenBank record **J02482.1** ([RefSeq](https://www.genome.jp/dbget-bin/www_bget?refseq+NC_001422); [Sanger-era sequence, PMID 870828](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/870828/); [J02482.1](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nucleotide/J02482.1)).\n\nPhiX174

compresses information through overlapping reading frames. **B lies within A**; **E lies within D**; **K overlaps A, B and C**; and **A\\*** is produced from an internal start within A. The structural block **J–F–G–H** is comparatively nonoverlapping, whereas

the other seven genes overlap at least one neighbor ([A/B evidence](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC432201/); [K evidence](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC288574/); [transcription map](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0042682220300957)).\n\n##

Established genes\n\nThe established set is **A, A\\*, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, J and K**. Concise conventional assignments ar[internal path] **A** — replication-associated protein; **A\\*** — internally initiated A product implicated in DNA binding, nuclease

protection and replication control.\n- **B** — procapsid assembly/scaffolding; **C** — replication/packaging-associated function; **D** — external scaffolding.\n- **E** — host-cell lysis; **F** — major capsid; **G** — major spike; **H** — DNA-pilot/minor structural

protein involved in adsorption and genome delivery; **J** — DNA-binding/internal capsid protein.
- **K** — nonessential accessory protein that can increase burst size/infectivity.

The supplied evidence directly supports A\*’s activities, H’s structural/entry

role and K’s nonessential phenotype ([A/A\\*](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P03631/entry); [H](https://www.snapgene.com/plasmids/basic_cloning_vectors/phiX174); [K, PMID 3155803](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3155803/)). The remaining brief assignments

are conventional but are not individually documented in the supplied excerpts and should therefore be treated as lower-confidence summaries.

## Transcription

The canonical model has promoters **P_A, P_B and P_D**. Four intrinsic (Rho-independent) terminators—**T_J,

T_F, T_G and T_H**—occur after J, F, G and H, respectively. They are leaky rather than absolute, allowing polymerase readthrough and progressively longer transcripts ([terminators/readthrough](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3335065/); [2020 map](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0042682220300957)).\n\nThe

2020 high-resolution infection transcript map broadly confirmed this model but reported a **putative promoter potentially recognized by heat-shock sigma factors** and revisited a controversial **Rho-dependent terminator**. Both remain **provisional**, not

equivalent to the canonical promoters and four intrinsic terminators ([2020 study, PMID 32560904](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32560904/); [institutional record](https://researchers.mq.edu.au/en/publications/a-high-resolution-map-of-bacteriophage-φx174-transcription/)).\n\n##

Established versus proposed coding capacity\n\nA 2019 synthesis-based study tested conserved cryptic ORFs and concluded that the annotation of **currently functional ORFs was complete**—that is, it established no additional functional ORF beyond the recognized

set. It also found regulatory suppression associated with **H expression**, illustrating that sequence conservation or an apparent ORF alone does not establish an extra gene. The H-specific experimental detail is not present in the supplied excerpts, so that

point cannot be characterized more precisely here ([Jaschke *et al.*, 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6883844/); [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1905990116)).
